screens.title: Securing Ansible Automation Platform Deployments
screens.narratorSegment: Security in automation is not optional. In this lesson you will learn the core controls an RHCA must design and operate to protect Ansible Automation Platform—how to grant the right access, securely store and inject secrets, collect trustworthy logs, and harden components and the infrastructure that runs them. I will show practical patterns: using Role-Based Access Control to avoid broad admin rights, using AAP credential types and Ansible Vault rather than hardcoded secrets, forwarding logs for forensic analysis and monitoring, and applying OS, network, and execution environment hardening. You will also understand FIPS considerations when the environment demands validated cryptography. Each topic includes an example you can apply, a common mistake to avoid, and a takeaway that ties back to compliance and operational safety. By the end you will be able to recommend RBAC mappings, design credential restrictions, instruct teams on secure playbook practices, and prioritize platform hardening steps for a production deployment. Think about one sensitive credential your organization manages now and how these controls would protect it.

screens.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
screens.narratorSegment: Role-Based Access Control is the primary way to restrict who can do what inside Ansible Controller. At its simplest, RBAC maps people and groups to permissions on specific resources. In AAP you model this with users (individual accounts), teams (groups of users), and organizations (top-level containers). Permissions such as read, write, execute, and admin are assigned to these entities on resources like projects, inventories, job templates, and credentials. A concrete example: create a team called AppDeployers that has execute permission on a staging deployment job template; those team members can run the job but cannot edit credentials or change the project code. A common mistake is to grant admin to many users so they can avoid permission errors; this violates the principle of least privilege and increases risk. When you design RBAC, create a matrix mapping organizational roles to the minimal set of permissions required for tasks, and review it regularly. Misconfigurations often arise from mixing permissions across multiple teams rather than relying on well-defined roles. Key takeaway: use users, teams, and organizations to make permissions explicit, auditable, and revoke-able. How would you map one of your teams to AAP roles right now?

keyIdea.text: Use users, teams, and organizations to assign minimal permissions on resources and avoid broad admin grants.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › RBAC
Definition
Role-Based Access Control
Map users and teams to precise permissions on Controller resources so automation tasks run with controlled authority.
Users, Teams, Organizations
Users are individuals, teams are groups, organizations are resource containers for separation.
Permissions
Assign read, write, execute, or admin on projects, inventories, templates, and credentials.
Common Mistake
Granting admin too broadly undermines audits and increases blast radius.
Key Takeaway

Design a permission matrix that maps roles to minimal permissions and review access regularly.

Structure
Organization
Top-level boundary for users and resources.
Team
Group users to simplify permission assignments.
User
Individual account with assigned team memberships and roles.
Permissions
Apply to resources: project, inventory, job template, credential.
Concrete Example
Create team AppDeployers; grant execute on "Deploy WebApp Staging" template; do not grant view or modify on credential used by the template. Team members run deployments, but cannot view raw keys or change the credential.

screens.title: Designing an RBAC Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: Designing an RBAC matrix is a repeatable process you can use for any automation program. Start by listing roles and responsibilities across your teams—developers, operators, security auditors, and SREs. Next, enumerate Controller resources those roles need: projects, inventories, job templates, credentials, and schedules. Third, assign minimal permissions—read, write, execute, or admin—per resource. For example, a developer may need read and execute on CI job templates, write access to project content only via pull requests, but not admin or credential modify rights. Fourth, implement the mappings in the Controller and test by impersonating or using test accounts. Finally, schedule periodic review and automated alerts for changes to high-risk permissions. A concrete pitfall to avoid is overlapping team memberships that unintentionally aggregate permissions and grant higher privileges than intended. Another common misconception is that fewer roles are always simpler; overly broad roles hide necessary granularity and complicate audits. Your outcome should be a clear, auditable matrix that can be reviewed during security assessments. Ask yourself: which resource changes should trigger an audit or approval workflow in your environment? Designing an RBAC Matrix means list roles and resources, assign minimal permissions, test with safe accounts, and review regularly to avoid privilege creep.. In practical terms, a step-by-step approach to least privilege mappings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › RBAC Matrix
Steps
  1. 1. Catalog roles and responsibilities across teams.
  2. 2. Enumerate Controller resources each role needs.
  3. 3. Assign minimal permissions per resource.
  4. 4. Implement, test with canary accounts, and document.
  5. 5. Schedule periodic reviews and alerts for high-privilege changes.
Misconception: fewer roles are always better—false. You need enough granularity to enforce least privilege without creating admin sprawl.
Example Mapping
AppDeployers
Execute on deploy templates; cannot view or modify credentials.
SecurityAuditors
Read-only access to job history and audit trails; no execute permissions.
BuildAdmins
Write access to projects and job templates; limited credential create rights.
PlatformAdmins
Admin on Controller for maintenance; membership should be small and audited.
Check: test account walkthrough
Use a test user in a candidate team to verify they can run required jobs and cannot view credential secrets or edit projects.
Key Takeaway

An RBAC matrix makes permissions auditable and reduces risk; avoid overlapping memberships that escalate privileges.

screens.title: Credential Management and Ansible Vault
screens.narratorSegment: Credential management is one of the most critical security responsibilities for automation. Ansible Vault provides encryption for static files and secrets at rest, but for runtime operations Ansible Automation Platform’s credential management centralizes secrets and injects them securely into execution environments. Controller credential types cover common secrets such as SSH private keys, cloud provider keys, tokens for HashiCorp Vault, or CyberArk connectors. When a job template runs, the Controller injects only the required secret material into the execution environment at runtime, so playbooks, logs, and environment variables do not contain plain-text secrets. A concrete example: store an SSH private key as a Machine credential in AAP; grant a team the use permission on that credential but do not grant view or change rights. A common misconception is that Ansible Vault alone is sufficient; in practice, Vault secures files but does not address runtime injection policies and RBAC controls offered by AAP. Best practice: never hardcode secrets in playbooks, restrict credential view and modify permissions, and rotate credentials regularly. Final thought: which credential in your project would benefit most from centralized AAP storage and stricter use permissions?

keyIdea.title: Store and inject secrets
keyIdea.text: Use Ansible Vault for files at rest and AAP credential types for runtime injection with RBAC on usage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Credential Management
Core Idea
Credentials and Vault
Centralize secrets in AAP and encrypt files with Ansible Vault when necessary; never leave keys in source control.
Credential Types
SSH, cloud providers, tokens, and custom types supported.
Runtime Injection
Controller injects secrets into execution environment only at job run time.
Common Mistake
Storing credentials in playbooks or plain Git without encryption.
Key Takeaway

Use AAP credentials for runtime secrets and Ansible Vault for at-rest encryption; apply RBAC to credential usage.

Credential Types (examples)
Machine (SSH)
SSH private keys for managed hosts.
Cloud Provider
AWS, Azure, GCP API keys and tokens.
HashiCorp / CyberArk
Third-party secrets managers and connectors.
Custom Types
Define fields for bespoke secret formats.
Concrete Example
Store your deployment SSH key as a Machine credential in Controller. Grant only the team 'use' permission on that credential. Do not grant 'view' or 'admin'. When the deploy job runs, the key is available inside the execution environment but is not written to logs or files in plain text.

screens.title: Credential Types and Runtime Injection
screens.narratorSegment: Controller credential types define the fields and behavior for secrets stored in the platform. When a job launches, the Controller authenticates to the execution environment and injects only the secrets required by that job. Architecturally, this separates secret storage from job runtime: the database holds encrypted secret blobs, RBAC governs who may use or view credentials, and the Controller performs secure runtime delivery. For example, a Machine credential holds an SSH private key; a job that runs against hosts uses the credential but cannot reveal the raw key to users who lack view permissions. Similarly, cloud credentials are injected into environment variables or connection plugins at runtime but are not stored in playbook repositories. A common misconception is that storing secrets in the Controller eliminates the need for rotation; in fact, you should rotate credentials regularly and audit usage. Another pitfall is failing to secure the Controller database and network paths; encrypted storage plus TLS for inter-component communication are both required for safety. Takeaway: trust in runtime injection relies on encryption at rest, strict RBAC on credential usage, and secure transport—verify each of these in your deployment.

keyIdea.title: Runtime injection model
keyIdea.text: Controller keeps encrypted credentials and injects necessary secrets into execution environments at job run time under RBAC control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Credential Injection
Flow
Encrypted store → RBAC check → Runtime injection
Controller stores encrypted credentials; when a job runs, Controller checks use permissions and delivers the secret into the execution environment, ensuring secrets never appear in plaintext in playbooks or logs.
Encryption at Rest
Database stores encrypted blobs for credentials.
RBAC
Use and view rights are distinct; grant minimal access.
Transport Security
TLS between Controller and execution nodes prevents interception.
Rotation
Rotate keys and tokens to limit exposure if a secret is compromised.
Example
A job template references a Machine credential containing an SSH private key. The Controller verifies the launching user or team has the 'use' role on the credential. The private key is injected into the execution environment only during execution. Team members can run the job but cannot view the underlying key unless explicitly granted view permissions.
Common Pitfalls
  • Relying on vault files alone without RBAC on runtime access.
  • Failing to restrict credential view permissions to a small trusted group.
  • Not encrypting Controller backups that contain credential blobs.
Key Takeaway

Secure runtime injection depends on encrypted storage, tight RBAC, transport security, and regular rotation.

screens.title: Conceptual awx-cli Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough presents conceptual awx-cli commands you would use to build a secure RBAC and credential setup. The commands create an organization, create a team and user, add the user to the team, create a project, create a Machine credential using an SSH key, and grant the team the 'use' and 'execute' roles on the credential and job template. A concrete example demonstrates that the user can execute the job but cannot view the SSH private key. A common misconception is to run such commands without validating permission boundaries; always check the effective permissions for the test user and ensure credential view access is not granted inadvertently. Also, do not paste real secrets in examples—treat CLI inputs as placeholders until the credential content is securely sourced. After executing these steps, verify the result by attempting to view the credential with a user who has only execute rights; they should be unable to retrieve raw key material. This process gives you a repeatable pattern to provision RBAC and credential usage safely in Controller. keyIdea.title: CLI pattern
keyIdea.text: Use awx-cli to create orgs, teams, users, projects, and credentials, and then grant minimal roles for use and execution.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › awx-cli Walkthrough
Conceptual Commands
# Create organization
awx-cli organizations create --name "DevOps Team"

# Create team
awx-cli teams create --name "AppDeployers" --organization "DevOps Team"

# Create user
awx-cli users create --username "devops_user" --password "SecurePassword123!" --email "devops@example.com" --first_name "DevOps" --last_name "User"

# Add user to team
awx-cli teams add_member --team "AppDeployers" --user "devops_user"

# Create project
awx-cli projects create --name "WebApp Deployment" --organization "DevOps Team" --scm_type git --scm_url "https://github.com/yourorg/webapp-playbooks.git" --scm_update_on_launch true

# Create credential (Machine)
# Assumes SSH key file at ~/.ssh/id_rsa_appdeploy
awx-cli credentials create --name "WebApp SSH Key" --organization "DevOps Team" --credential_type "Machine" --inputs "ssh_key_data=$(cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa_appdeploy)" --inputs "username=ansible"

# Grant team use on credential
awx-cli credentials grant_role --role "use" --credential "WebApp SSH Key" --team "AppDeployers"

# Create job template and grant execute
awx-cli job_templates create --name "Deploy WebApp Staging" --project "WebApp Deployment" --inventory "Staging Inventory" --credential "WebApp SSH Key" --playbook "deploy_staging.yml" --organization "DevOps Team"
awx-cli job_templates grant_role --role "execute" --job_template "Deploy WebApp Staging" --team "AppDeployers"
Explanation & Checks
  • After creation, verify that the team only has the 'use' role on the credential and 'execute' on the job template.
  • Log in as devops_user to confirm they can launch the job but cannot view the SSH key material.
  • Rotate the SSH key and update the credential periodically to reduce exposure time.
Common Mistakes
Pasting real private keys into example commands or granting view permissions to too many users.
Key Takeaway

Use awx-cli to automate secure setup, then validate effective permissions with test accounts before production use.

screens.title: Auditing and Logging for Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: Auditing and logging are essential for compliance and incident response. AAP provides built-in logs for job runs, user actions, configuration changes, and A P I activity. To make logs useful for forensic analysis, you should centralize them in a secure, tamper-evident system like a SIEM so data from multiple Controllers and system components can be correlated. Ensure logs are protected against unauthorized modification and retained according to policy. Practical steps include configuring Controller to forward syslog, securing network channels for log transport, and applying access controls to the log archive. A common misconception is that local Controller logs alone are sufficient; local logs are useful but vulnerable to tampering or accidental deletion. Also avoid keeping logs only for short windows; compliance often requires longer retention. For monitoring, create alerts for suspicious patterns such as repeated failed logins, unexpected changes to credentials or RBAC, and anomalous job executions. A concrete example: forward /var/log/tower/ entries to your SIEM and set alerts for credential modification events. Takeaway: centralize, protect, retain, and monitor logs so automation activity is auditable and actionable. Auditing and Logging for Compliance means forward and protect aap logs to a central siem for long-term retention, correlation, and monitoring to support compliance.. In practical terms, collect, protect, and monitor aap logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Forwarding Logs to SIEM
screens.narratorSegment: Forwarding Controller logs to a SIEM involves a sequence of steps that ensure completeness, security, and usefulness. First, identify the log sources you need: job events, A P I calls, auth events, and system logs. Second, configure the Controller to forward logs via syslog or a supported integration, making sure transport uses TLS to protect data in flight. Third, map log fields in the SIEM so events are searchable and correlated across systems. Fourth, apply retention and protection policies to the log store and restrict who can edit forwarding rules. Fifth, create monitoring rules and alerting for suspicious events such as mass login failures, unexpected credential modifications, or large-scale job runs. A concrete monitoring scenario: an alert that fires when a normally low-volume user executes hundreds of jobs in a short window, which might indicate compromised automation. A common misconception is that forwarding logs is a one-time task; it should be part of change control and reviewed after upgrades to Controller or logging infrastructure. Final step: test your alerting by simulating safe, controlled events to validate detection and investigation playbooks.

screens.title: Hardening AAP Components
screens.narratorSegment: Hardening the platform and its underlying infrastructure reduces attack surface and supports secure operation. At the operating system level, apply security baselines such as CIS, keep RHEL patched, disable unnecessary services, and enable host-level firewalls. On the network, use segmentation to limit which hosts and ports Controller, Automation Hub, and Execution Nodes can access. Use TLS for all inter-component traffic. For the database, enforce strong passwords, restrict network access to the database server, and ensure backups are encrypted and protected. Execution environments should be built from minimal, trusted base images, regularly updated, and scanned for vulnerabilities. A concrete comparison: a hardened execution environment contains only the runtime libraries needed by your playbooks, while an un-hardened image may include development tools and extra dependencies that increase vulnerability surface. Common misconception: patching only the Controller is sufficient; unpatched execution nodes or database servers remain risk vectors. Key practical step: create a checklist for each component—OS baseline, network rules, DB hardening, EE image validation—and integrate these checks into your release and upgrade processes. screens.title: FIPS Compliance for AAP
screens.narratorSegment: FIPS compliance requires that cryptographic operations use validated algorithms and modules. For an AAP deployment, achieving FIPS mode typically begins by enabling FIPS on the underlying RHEL operating systems that host Controller, Automation Hub, and Execution Nodes. Once the OS is in FIPS mode, ensure that AAP components and the database are configured to use the FIPS-validated libraries provided by the distribution. An important distinction: enabling FIPS at the OS level is necessary but not sufficient by itself; you must verify that every component and integration uses FIPS-validated cryptography, including connectors and third-party libraries. A concrete example: if a custom connector uses a non-validated crypto module, that component may break FIPS compliance even if the OS is compliant. A common misconception is that flipping a single flag makes the entire automation stack compliant. Instead, treat FIPS as a project: inventory cryptographic dependencies, update to validated libraries, run validation tests, and document the configuration for audit. Takeaway: FIPS readiness requires coordinated changes across OS, AAP components, and any integrations that perform cryptographic operations. FIPS Compliance for AAP means enable fips on os and confirm that all aap components and integrations use fips-validated cryptography.. In practical terms, validated cryptography and platform considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Continuous Security: Audits, Scans, and Patch Management
screens.narratorSegment: Security is continuous. Regular audits, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, and timely patching are all part of a secure AAP lifecycle. Start with scheduled vulnerability scans of Controller hosts, execution environments, and the database. Run container image scans on Execution Environment images before they are used in production. Conduct periodic penetration tests against your automation interfaces and review findings. Maintain an upgrade and patch plan that prioritizes security fixes, and ensure test environments validate changes before production rollout. A concrete example: when Red Hat publishes a security advisory affecting a dependency used by your EEs, scan all EEs, rebuild affected images from patched bases, and roll them out through your deployment pipeline. A common misconception is that patching can wait indefinitely during busy periods; delaying fixes increases exposure and undermines compliance. Finally, document and track remediation activities and integrate those actions into your change management process. Takeaway: build an operational rhythm for scanning, testing, patching, and verifying to keep the automation platform resilient to evolving threats. fullNarratorScript:
Security in automation is not optional. In this lesson you will learn the core controls an RHCA must design and operate to protect Ansible Automation Platform—how to grant the right access, securely store and inject secrets, collect trustworthy logs, and harden components and the infrastructure that runs them. I will show practical patterns: using Role-Based Access Control to avoid broad admin rights, using AAP credential types and Ansible Vault rather than hardcoded secrets, forwarding logs for forensic analysis and monitoring, and applying OS, network, and execution environment hardening. You will also understand FIPS considerations when the environment demands validated cryptography. Each topic includes an example you can apply, a common mistake to avoid, and a takeaway that ties back to compliance and operational safety. By the end you will be able to recommend RBAC mappings, design credential restrictions, instruct teams on secure playbook practices, and prioritize platform hardening steps for a production deployment. Think about one sensitive credential your organization manages now and how these controls would protect it.

These objectives describe the concrete skills you will gain. First, you will implement Role-Based Access Control inside the Ansible Controller to set granular permissions for users, teams, and organizations, so automation tasks run with least privilege. Second, you will manage and secure sensitive credentials using Ansible Vault and AAP's credential types so secrets are never stored in plain text or exposed during execution. Third, you will configure auditing and logging so that every job execution, user action, and configuration change can be reviewed, retained, and forwarded to centralized systems for analysis. Fourth, you will harden the platform and underlying infrastructure by applying OS and network controls, securing the database, and ensuring execution environments come from trusted, scanned images. Each objective links to a practical milestone: mapping roles, creating restricted credentials, forwarding logs to a SIEM, and applying hardening baselines. These are the tasks you will be expected to demonstrate in a production design review, and they map directly to compliance and operational risk reduction. Consider which objective you need to practice first in your environment.

These follow-on objectives build the tactical knowledge you will need as an architect. First, you will be able to configure FIPS-compliant deployments by enabling validated cryptographic libraries across the operating system and AAP components, which is essential for regulated environments. Second, you will apply the principle of least privilege when mapping roles and credential access so that teams can perform their tasks but cannot escalate or exfiltrate secrets. Third, you will secure execution environments by using trusted base images, removing unnecessary packages, and scanning images for vulnerabilities before deployment. Fourth, you will operationalize logging retention and monitoring so that logs are protected, tamper-evident, and retained per policy for forensic readiness. Together these objectives form a checklist you can use during design reviews and audits. Think about which of these four checkpoints your current deployment is weakest at and plan a small first improvement to make this week.

Role-Based Access Control is the primary way to restrict who can do what inside Ansible Controller. At its simplest, RBAC maps people and groups to permissions on specific resources. In AAP you model this with users (individual accounts), teams (groups of users), and organizations (top-level containers). Permissions such as read, write, execute, and admin are assigned to these entities on resources like projects, inventories, job templates, and credentials. A concrete example: create a team called AppDeployers that has execute permission on a staging deployment job template; those team members can run the job but cannot edit credentials or change the project code. A common mistake is to grant admin to many users so they can avoid permission errors; this violates the principle of least privilege and increases risk. When you design RBAC, create a matrix mapping organizational roles to the minimal set of permissions required for tasks, and review it regularly. Misconfigurations often arise from mixing permissions across multiple teams rather than relying on well-defined roles. Key takeaway: use users, teams, and organizations to make permissions explicit, auditable, and revoke-able. How would you map one of your teams to AAP roles right now?

Designing an RBAC matrix is a repeatable process you can use for any automation program. Start by listing roles and responsibilities across your teams—developers, operators, security auditors, and SREs. Next, enumerate Controller resources those roles need: projects, inventories, job templates, credentials, and schedules. Third, assign minimal permissions—read, write, execute, or admin—per resource. For example, a developer may need read and execute on CI job templates, write access to project content only via pull requests, but not admin or credential modify rights. Fourth, implement the mappings in the Controller and test by impersonating or using test accounts. Finally, schedule periodic review and automated alerts for changes to high-risk permissions. A concrete pitfall to avoid is overlapping team memberships that unintentionally aggregate permissions and grant higher privileges than intended. Another common misconception is that fewer roles are always simpler; overly broad roles hide necessary granularity and complicate audits. Your outcome should be a clear, auditable matrix that can be reviewed during security assessments. Ask yourself: which resource changes should trigger an audit or approval workflow in your environment? Designing an RBAC Matrix means list roles and resources, assign minimal permissions, test with safe accounts, and review regularly to avoid privilege creep.. In practical terms, a step-by-step approach to least privilege mappings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Credential management is one of the most critical security responsibilities for automation. Ansible Vault provides encryption for static files and secrets at rest, but for runtime operations Ansible Automation Platform’s credential management centralizes secrets and injects them securely into execution environments. Controller credential types cover common secrets such as SSH private keys, cloud provider keys, tokens for HashiCorp Vault, or CyberArk connectors. When a job template runs, the Controller injects only the required secret material into the execution environment at runtime, so playbooks, logs, and environment variables do not contain plain-text secrets. A concrete example: store an SSH private key as a Machine credential in AAP; grant a team the use permission on that credential but do not grant view or change rights. A common misconception is that Ansible Vault alone is sufficient; in practice, Vault secures files but does not address runtime injection policies and RBAC controls offered by AAP. Best practice: never hardcode secrets in playbooks, restrict credential view and modify permissions, and rotate credentials regularly. Final thought: which credential in your project would benefit most from centralized AAP storage and stricter use permissions?

Controller credential types define the fields and behavior for secrets stored in the platform. When a job launches, the Controller authenticates to the execution environment and injects only the secrets required by that job. Architecturally, this separates secret storage from job runtime: the database holds encrypted secret blobs, RBAC governs who may use or view credentials, and the Controller performs secure runtime delivery. For example, a Machine credential holds an SSH private key; a job that runs against hosts uses the credential but cannot reveal the raw key to users who lack view permissions. Similarly, cloud credentials are injected into environment variables or connection plugins at runtime but are not stored in playbook repositories. A common misconception is that storing secrets in the Controller eliminates the need for rotation; in fact, you should rotate credentials regularly and audit usage. Another pitfall is failing to secure the Controller database and network paths; encrypted storage plus TLS for inter-component communication are both required for safety. Takeaway: trust in runtime injection relies on encryption at rest, strict RBAC on credential usage, and secure transport—verify each of these in your deployment.

The commands create an organization, create a team and user, add the user to the team, create a project, create a Machine credential using an SSH key, and grant the team the 'use' and 'execute' roles on the credential and job template. This process gives you a repeatable pattern to provision RBAC and credential usage safely in Controller.
